title: Observers & Compensators
description: Estimate the states you cannot measure, then combine the estimator with state feedback into one compensator.

study.title: Why an estimator?
study.body: State feedback needs every state, but sensors usually measure only $y$. Differentiating $y$ to get velocities amplifies noise. Instead, run a copy of the model in the computer, driven by the same $u$. On its own that copy is an **open-loop** estimator: its error obeys $\dot{\tilde{\mathbf{x}}} = \mathbf{A}\tilde{\mathbf{x}}$, so it converges only as fast as the plant, and never for an unstable plant. The fix: correct the copy with the measured output error.

study.title: The full-order estimator
study.body: The model copy is corrected by $\mathbf{L}$ times the output error $y - \mathbf{C}\hat{\mathbf{x}}$. Subtracting from the plant equation, $u$ cancels and the error obeys $\dot{\tilde{\mathbf{x}}} = (\mathbf{A} - \mathbf{L}\mathbf{C})\tilde{\mathbf{x}}$. Choose $\mathbf{L}$ so that $\mathbf{A} - \mathbf{L}\mathbf{C}$ has fast, stable eigenvalues and $\hat{\mathbf{x}}$ locks onto $\mathbf{x}$ from any starting guess.

study.title: Choosing L
study.body:
Match $\det(s\mathbf{I} - \mathbf{A} + \mathbf{L}\mathbf{C})$ with the desired estimator polynomial $\alpha_e(s)$.
**Example:** double integrator with position sensor, $\mathbf{C} = [1 \;\; 0]$: $\mathbf{A} - \mathbf{L}\mathbf{C} = \begin{bmatrix} -l_1 & 1 \\ -l_2 & 0 \end{bmatrix}$ with polynomial $s^2 + l_1s + l_2$. Estimator poles at $-10 \pm 10j$: $s^2 + 20s + 200$, so $\mathbf{L} = [20 \;\; 200]^T$.

study.title: Duality
study.body: $\mathbf{A} - \mathbf{L}\mathbf{C}$ has the same eigenvalues as its transpose $\mathbf{A}^T - \mathbf{C}^T\mathbf{L}^T$: a pole-placement problem for the pair $(\mathbf{A}^T, \mathbf{C}^T)$ with gain $\mathbf{L}^T$. So everything from unit 4 carries over: $\mathbf{L}$ exists for any poles exactly when $(\mathbf{A}, \mathbf{C})$ is observable. In observer canonical form each gain is simply $l_i = \alpha_i - a_i$, and Ackermann's formula becomes the one below.

study.title: How fast should the estimator be?
study.body: The estimation error should die out before it disturbs the controlled response, so a common rule (FPE) puts the estimator poles about **2 to 6 times further from the origin** than the controller poles. Much faster needs a large $\mathbf{L}$, which feeds sensor noise straight into $\hat{\mathbf{x}}$ and into $u$. Slower poles make the estimate lag. With a noisy sensor, choose the slower end; with a clean sensor and a fast actuator, the faster end.

study.title: Explore: estimator speed
study.body: A first-order plant $\dot x = -x + u$, $y = x$, with estimator gain $\ell$. The estimate starts 1 off; the error decays as $e^{-(1+\ell)t}$ whatever the input does. With $\ell = 0$ (open-loop copy) it only decays at the plant's own rate.

study.title: Separation principle
study.body: Now feed back the estimate: $u = -\mathbf{K}\hat{\mathbf{x}} + \bar Nr$. In the coordinates $(\mathbf{x}, \tilde{\mathbf{x}})$ the closed-loop matrix is block triangular, so its eigenvalues are those of $\mathbf{A} - \mathbf{B}\mathbf{K}$ (controller) together with those of $\mathbf{A} - \mathbf{L}\mathbf{C}$ (estimator). Design $\mathbf{K}$ and $\mathbf{L}$ separately; the combination works. If $r$ enters plant and estimator through the same $u$, the estimator poles cancel from $Y(s)/R(s)$.

study.title: The compensator
study.body: Estimator plus state feedback together form a dynamic controller from $y$ to $u$, with the transfer function below ($r = 0$, $U = -D_c(s)Y$). Its poles are the eigenvalues of $\mathbf{A} - \mathbf{B}\mathbf{K} - \mathbf{L}\mathbf{C}$, not the closed-loop poles. For the double integrator it comes out as a lead compensator: state-space design rediscovers lead compensation.

steps.title: Why estimate the state?
steps.body: Pole placement needs every state, but a typical plant has one sensor. The idea: simulate the plant in the controller with the same input $u$ and use the simulated states $\hat{\mathbf{x}}$. A pure copy has error dynamics $\dot{\tilde{\mathbf{x}}} = \mathbf{A}\tilde{\mathbf{x}}$, which is as slow as the plant, or unstable.

steps.prompt: An open-loop estimator (a model copy driven by $u$, without output correction) works for an unstable plant, as long as the model is exact.
steps.explanation: With an exact model the error still obeys $\dot{\tilde{\mathbf{x}}} = \mathbf{A}\tilde{\mathbf{x}}$. Any initial guess error $\tilde{\mathbf{x}}(0) \ne \mathbf{0}$ (and in practice you never know $\mathbf{x}(0)$ exactly) grows with the unstable mode. Only feedback from the measurement, $\mathbf{L}(y - \mathbf{C}\hat{\mathbf{x}})$, can move the error dynamics.

steps.title: The closed-loop estimator
steps.body: Correct the copy with the output error: $\dot{\hat{\mathbf{x}}} = \mathbf{A}\hat{\mathbf{x}} + \mathbf{B}u + \mathbf{L}(y - \mathbf{C}\hat{\mathbf{x}})$. Subtract it from $\dot{\mathbf{x}} = \mathbf{A}\mathbf{x} + \mathbf{B}u$: the input cancels and the error obeys the equation below. $\mathbf{L}$ sets the estimator poles, just as $\mathbf{K}$ set the controller poles.

steps.prompt: A first-order plant $\dot x = ax + bu$ with $a$ = {{a}}, $b$ = {{b}} has sensor $y = cx$ with $c$ = {{c}}. Which estimator gain $\ell$ puts the estimator pole at $s = -{{p}}$?
steps.explanation: Error dynamics: $\dot{\tilde x} = (a - \ell c)\tilde x$, pole at ${{a}} - {{c}}\ell$. Set it to −{{p}}: $\ell = \frac{a + p}{c} = \frac{ {{a}} + {{p}} }{ {{c}} }$ = {{(a + p)/c}}. The input gain $b$ plays no role: $u$ cancels from the error equation.

steps.title: Two states, one sensor
steps.body: For $\mathbf{A} = \begin{bmatrix} 0 & 1 \\ -a_0 & -a_1 \end{bmatrix}$ and a position sensor $\mathbf{C} = [1 \;\; 0]$, $\mathbf{L}\mathbf{C}$ only fills the first column: $\mathbf{A} - \mathbf{L}\mathbf{C} = \begin{bmatrix} -l_1 & 1 \\ -a_0 - l_2 & -a_1 \end{bmatrix}$. Its polynomial is below; match it with $\alpha_e(s)$, first $l_1$, then $l_2$.

steps.prompt: $\mathbf{A} = \begin{bmatrix} 0 & 1 \\ {{-a0}} & {{-a1}} \end{bmatrix}$, $\mathbf{C} = [1 \;\; 0]$. Place the estimator poles at $-{{p1}}$ and $-{{p2}}$.
Duality: match each controller quantity to its estimator counterpart.
steps.explanation: Transpose $\mathbf{A} - \mathbf{L}\mathbf{C}$ to get $\mathbf{A}^T - \mathbf{C}^T\mathbf{L}^T$, which has the same eigenvalues. That is state feedback for the plant $(\mathbf{A}^T, \mathbf{C}^T)$ with gain $\mathbf{L}^T$; its controllability matrix is $\mathcal{O}^T$. Every pole-placement tool works for estimators after this swap.

steps.prompt: The controller poles are at $-2 \pm 2j$. Which estimator poles follow the usual design rule?
steps.explanation: Put the estimator poles roughly 2 to 6 times further from the origin than the controller poles: $-8 \pm 8j$ is 4 times. Slower poles ($-1 \pm j$) make the estimate lag behind and spoil the response; equal ones barely help; 100 times faster needs a huge $\mathbf{L}$ that feeds sensor noise into $u$.

steps.prompt: Plant $\dot x = -x + u$ with sensor $y = x$. Set the estimator gain $\ell$ so that the estimation error has dropped to about 2 % after {{T|s}}.
steps.explanation: The error obeys $\dot{\tilde x} = -(1 + \ell)\tilde x$, so it falls to $e^{-4} \approx$ 2 % at $t = 4/(1 + \ell)$. Setting this to {{T|s}}: $1 + \ell$ = {{4/T}}, so $\ell$ = {{4/T - 1}}. The open-loop copy ($\ell = 0$) would need 4 s.

steps.title: Separation principle
steps.body: Use the estimate for feedback: $u = -\mathbf{K}\hat{\mathbf{x}} + \bar Nr$. Write the closed loop in $\mathbf{x}$ and $\tilde{\mathbf{x}}$: the matrix is block triangular with $\mathbf{A} - \mathbf{B}\mathbf{K}$ and $\mathbf{A} - \mathbf{L}\mathbf{C}$ on the diagonal. So the $2n$ closed-loop poles are simply the controller poles plus the estimator poles.

steps.prompt: A second-order plant gets a controller with $\alpha_c(s) = s^2 + {{c1}}s + {{c0}}$ and a full-order estimator with $\alpha_e(s) = s^2 + {{e1}}s + {{e0}}$. The closed loop is fourth order: $s^4 + \beta_3s^3 + \beta_2s^2 + \beta_1s + \beta_0$.

ask.explanation: By the separation principle the closed-loop polynomial is $\alpha_c(s)\alpha_e(s)$. The $s^3$ terms come from $s^2\cdot{{e1}}s + {{c1}}s\cdot s^2$: $\beta_3$ = {{c1}} + {{e1}} = {{c1 + e1}}.
Closed-loop polynomial $\alpha_c(s)\alpha_e(s)$; its constant term is the product of the constant terms: {{c0}} × {{e0}} = {{c0*e0}}.

steps.prompt: With $u = -\mathbf{K}\hat{\mathbf{x}} + \bar Nr$ and the estimator driven by that same $u$, the estimator poles appear as poles of the transfer function from $r$ to $y$.
steps.explanation: The estimation error obeys $\dot{\tilde{\mathbf{x}}} = (\mathbf{A} - \mathbf{L}\mathbf{C})\tilde{\mathbf{x}}$ with no $r$ in it: the error modes are **uncontrollable from** $r$. Uncontrollable modes cancel from the transfer function, so $Y(s)/R(s) = \bar N\frac{N(s)}{\alpha_c(s)}$, exactly as with full-state feedback. The estimator poles still matter for disturbances, noise and initial errors.

steps.title: The compensator
steps.body: Seen from outside, the estimator plus the gain $\mathbf{K}$ is just a dynamic controller that takes $y$ and produces $u$: $\dot{\hat{\mathbf{x}}} = (\mathbf{A} - \mathbf{B}\mathbf{K} - \mathbf{L}\mathbf{C})\hat{\mathbf{x}} + \mathbf{L}y$, $u = -\mathbf{K}\hat{\mathbf{x}}$ (for $r = 0$). Its own poles are the eigenvalues of $\mathbf{A} - \mathbf{B}\mathbf{K} - \mathbf{L}\mathbf{C}$; they need not even be stable. In transfer-function form $U(s) = -D_c(s)Y(s)$ with $D_c(s)$ below.

steps.prompt: First-order plant $\dot x = ax + bu$ ($a$ = {{a}}, $b$ = {{b}}), $y = x$, with state-feedback gain $k$ = {{k}} and estimator gain $\ell$ = {{l}}. The compensator is $\dot{\hat x} = (a - bk - \ell)\hat x + \ell y$, $u = -k\hat x$.

ask.prompt: Find the pole of the compensator.
ask.explanation: The compensator state $\hat x$ has the dynamics $a - bk - \ell$ = {{a}} − {{b}}·{{k}} − {{l}} = {{a - b*k - l}}. Compare: the closed-loop poles are $a - bk$ = {{a - b*k}} (controller) and $a - \ell$ = {{a - l}} (estimator). The compensator pole is neither.
$\frac{U}{Y} = \frac{-k\ell}{s - (a - bk - \ell)}$. At $s = 0$: $\frac{-{{k}}\cdot{{l}}}{ {{-(a - b*k - l)}} }$ = {{-k*l/(-(a - b*k - l))}}. The minus sign is the negative feedback: $u$ opposes $y$.

steps.prompt: Put the steps of an observer-based (compensator) design in order.
items: Choose controller poles from the specs and compute $\mathbf{K}$
Choose estimator poles 2–6× faster and compute $\mathbf{L}$
Check robustness and noise in simulation
steps.explanation: Controllability is needed for $\mathbf{K}$, observability for $\mathbf{L}$. By the separation principle $\mathbf{K}$ and $\mathbf{L}$ can be designed one after the other; the estimator poles are chosen relative to the controller poles, so $\mathbf{K}$ comes first. $\bar N$ follows from the final loop. Separation guarantees the poles, not robustness, so always check margins and noise.

steps.prompt: $G(s) = \frac{b_1s + b_2}{s^2 + {{a1}}s + {{a2}}}$ is realized in observer canonical form ($\mathbf{A}_o = \begin{bmatrix} -{{a1}} & 1 \\ -{{a2}} & 0 \end{bmatrix}$, $\mathbf{C}_o = [1 \;\; 0]$). Place the estimator poles at $-{{sg}} \pm j{{w}}$.

ask.explanation: $\mathbf{A}_o - \mathbf{L}\mathbf{C}_o = \begin{bmatrix} -{{a1}} - l_1 & 1 \\ -{{a2}} - l_2 & 0 \end{bmatrix}$ has polynomial $s^2 + ({{a1}} + l_1)s + ({{a2}} + l_2)$, so $l_i = \alpha_i - a_i$. Desired $(s + {{sg}})^2 + {{w}}^2 = s^2 + {{2*sg}}s + {{sg^2 + w^2}}$: $l_1$ = {{2*sg}} − {{a1}} = {{2*sg - a1}}.
In observer canonical form $l_i = \alpha_i - a_i$. $\alpha_2 = \sigma^2 + \omega^2$ = {{sg^2 + w^2}}, so $l_2$ = {{sg^2 + w^2}} − {{a2}} = {{sg^2 + w^2 - a2}}.

steps.prompt: The estimator needs the plant input $u$ as well as the measurement $y$.
steps.explanation: The model copy contains $\mathbf{B}u$. That term is what makes $u$ cancel in the error equation $\dot{\tilde{\mathbf{x}}} = (\mathbf{A} - \mathbf{L}\mathbf{C})\tilde{\mathbf{x}}$. Without it, every change in $u$ would show up as estimation error. In a compensator the controller knows $u$ anyway, because it computes it.

steps.prompt: Double integrator with position sensor: $\mathbf{A} = \begin{bmatrix} 0 & 1 \\ 0 & 0 \end{bmatrix}$, $\mathbf{C} = [1 \;\; 0]$. Place the estimator poles at $\zeta$ = {{zt}}, $\omega_n$ = {{wn}} rad/s.

ask.explanation: Polynomial $s^2 + l_1s + l_2$; match the constant term: $l_2 = \omega_n^2$ = {{wn^2}}. It is large because a fast estimator needs a strong correction of the velocity estimate.

steps.prompt: $\mathbf{A} = \begin{bmatrix} {{a11}} & {{a12}} \\ {{a21}} & {{a22}} \end{bmatrix}$, $\mathbf{C} = [1 \;\; 0]$. Place the estimator poles at $-{{p1}}$ and $-{{p2}}$.

A double-integrator controller has its poles at $\zeta = 0.7$, $\omega_n$ = {{wnc}} rad/s. The estimator ($\mathbf{C} = [1 \;\; 0]$) gets $\zeta = 0.7$ and an $\omega_n$ {{c}} times larger. Find $l_2$.
steps.explanation: Estimator: $\omega_n$ = {{c}} × {{wnc}} = {{c*wnc}} rad/s. For the double integrator $s^2 + l_1s + l_2$ must equal $s^2 + 2\zeta\omega_ns + \omega_n^2$, so $l_2 = \omega_n^2$ = {{(c*wnc)^2}} (and $l_1$ = {{1.4*c*wnc}}). Doubling the speed factor quadruples $l_2$: more noise reaches the velocity estimate.

steps.prompt: Use the estimator version of Ackermann's formula, $\mathbf{L} = \alpha_e(\mathbf{A})\mathcal{O}^{-1}[0 \;\; 1]^T$, for $\mathbf{A} = \begin{bmatrix} {{a}} & 1 \\ 0 & {{d}} \end{bmatrix}$, $\mathbf{C} = [1 \;\; 0]$ and estimator poles $-{{p1}}$, $-{{p2}}$. Find $l_2$.
steps.explanation:
$\mathcal{O} = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 \\ {{a}} & 1 \end{bmatrix}$, $\mathcal{O}^{-1} = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 \\ {{-a}} & 1 \end{bmatrix}$, so $\mathcal{O}^{-1}[0 \;\; 1]^T = [0 \;\; 1]^T$ and $\mathbf{L}$ is the **second column** of $\alpha_e(\mathbf{A}) = \mathbf{A}^2 + {{p1+p2}}\mathbf{A} + {{p1*p2}}\mathbf{I}$.
Second column of $\mathbf{A}^2$: $[{{a + d}} \;\; {{d^2}}]^T$, of $\mathbf{A}$: $[1 \;\; {{d}}]^T$. Bottom entry: $l_2$ = {{d^2}} + {{p1+p2}}·({{d}}) + {{p1*p2}} = {{d^2 + (p1 + p2)*d + p1*p2}} (and $l_1$ = {{a + d + p1 + p2}}).

steps.prompt: The estimator poles are moved much further left (larger $\mathbf{L}$). What is the main price?
options: Sensor noise is amplified into $\hat{\mathbf{x}}$ and the control signal
The controller poles move as well
The steady-state error to a step grows
steps.explanation: $\mathbf{L}$ multiplies the measured $y$, including its noise, so a large $\mathbf{L}$ injects that noise into $\hat{\mathbf{x}}$ and through $\mathbf{K}$ into $u$. The controller poles do not move (separation principle), the reference response is unchanged (the estimator poles cancel from $Y/R$), and observability is a property of the plant, not of $\mathbf{L}$.

steps.prompt: An estimator can be designed for an unstable plant, as long as $(\mathbf{A}, \mathbf{C})$ is observable.
steps.explanation: Observability guarantees that $\mathbf{L}$ can place all eigenvalues of $\mathbf{A} - \mathbf{L}\mathbf{C}$ anywhere, including in the left half-plane, whatever $\mathbf{A}$ itself does. The output correction pulls $\hat{\mathbf{x}}$ along with the diverging state. That is exactly why the open-loop copy fails and the closed-loop estimator works.

steps.prompt: Double integrator $\mathbf{A} = \begin{bmatrix} 0 & 1 \\ 0 & 0 \end{bmatrix}$, $\mathbf{B} = [0 \;\; 1]^T$, $\mathbf{C} = [1 \;\; 0]$ with $\mathbf{K} = [{{k1}} \;\; {{k2}}]$ and $\mathbf{L} = [{{l1}} \;\; {{l2}}]^T$. Working out $D_c(s)$ from the study card gives $D_c(s) = \frac{(k_1l_1 + k_2l_2)s + k_1l_2}{s^2 + (l_1 + k_2)s + l_1k_2 + k_1 + l_2}$.

ask.explanation: Numerator $({{k1}}\cdot{{l1}} + {{k2}}\cdot{{l2}})s + {{k1}}\cdot{{l2}}$ = ${{k1*l1 + k2*l2}}s + {{k1*l2}}$, zero at $s$ = −{{k1*l2}}/{{k1*l1 + k2*l2}} = {{-k1*l2/(k1*l1 + k2*l2)}}. The two compensator poles, roots of $s^2 + {{l1 + k2}}s + {{l1*k2 + k1 + l2}}$, lie much further from the origin (magnitude $\sqrt{ {{l1*k2 + k1 + l2}} }$ = {{sqrt(l1*k2 + k1 + l2)}}): the compensator acts like a lead network.

steps.prompt: For the same double integrator with $\mathbf{K} = [{{k1}} \;\; {{k2}}]$ and $\mathbf{L} = [{{l1}} \;\; {{l2}}]^T$, the closed loop with states $(\mathbf{x}, \hat{\mathbf{x}})$ is fourth order: $s^4 + \beta_3s^3 + \beta_2s^2 + \beta_1s + \beta_0$.

The balancing robot $\mathbf{A} = \begin{bmatrix} 0 & 1 \\ {{W^2}} & 0 \end{bmatrix}$ measures only its tilt, $\mathbf{C} = [1 \;\; 0]$. Place the estimator poles at $-{{p1}}$ and $-{{p2}}$. Find $l_2$.
steps.explanation: $\mathbf{A} - \mathbf{L}\mathbf{C} = \begin{bmatrix} -l_1 & 1 \\ {{W^2}} - l_2 & 0 \end{bmatrix}$, polynomial $s^2 + l_1s + (l_2 - {{W^2}})$. Match $(s + {{p1}})(s + {{p2}}) = s^2 + {{p1+p2}}s + {{p1*p2}}$: $l_2$ = {{p1*p2}} + {{W^2}} = {{p1*p2 + W^2}}. Part of $l_2$ cancels the unstable term, as in the controller design.

steps.prompt: The reference enters as $u = -\mathbf{K}\hat{\mathbf{x}} + \bar Nr$ and the estimator is driven by that $u$. Which poles appear in $Y(s)/R(s)$?
options: Only the controller poles, the eigenvalues of $\mathbf{A} - \mathbf{B}\mathbf{K}$
Only the estimator poles, the eigenvalues of $\mathbf{A} - \mathbf{L}\mathbf{C}$
Both the controller and the estimator poles
The compensator poles, the eigenvalues of $\mathbf{A} - \mathbf{B}\mathbf{K} - \mathbf{L}\mathbf{C}$
steps.explanation: The error $\tilde{\mathbf{x}}$ obeys $\dot{\tilde{\mathbf{x}}} = (\mathbf{A} - \mathbf{L}\mathbf{C})\tilde{\mathbf{x}}$ without any $r$, so a reference step never excites it: those modes are uncontrollable from $r$ and cancel. $Y/R = \bar N\frac{N(s)}{\alpha_c(s)}$, the same as with measured states. (If instead $r$ entered as an error $r - y$ into the compensator, the estimator poles would in general show up.)

steps.prompt: $G(s) = \frac{1}{s^3 + {{a1}}s^2 + {{a2}}s + {{a3}}}$ is realized in observer canonical form. Put all three estimator poles at $s = -{{p}}$. Find $l_3$.
If $(\mathbf{A}, \mathbf{C})$ is not observable, no estimator gain $\mathbf{L}$ can make the estimation error go to zero.
steps.explanation: The unobservable modes are eigenvalues of $\mathbf{A} - \mathbf{L}\mathbf{C}$ for every $\mathbf{L}$: they cannot be moved. If they are **stable** (the system is detectable), the error in those directions still decays, just at the plant's own rate, and the estimate converges. Only an unstable unobservable mode makes estimation impossible.
